transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Lina Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Reyes (Nimbus CTO), Priya Singh (Nimbus ML), Jordan Lee (Nimbus Infra)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood did a deep dive into GPU runtime profiling across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM. We discussed kernel selection, how CUDA graphs reduce kernel launch overhead for short sequences and high qps, KV cache hit/miss patterns with prefix caching, and quantization tradeoffs. Action items: share benchmarks, Nimbus to share model+prompts, schedule a live run.

[00:00] Lina: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick round of intros?
[00:08] Alex: Hi, Alex Reyes here - CTO at Nimbus. We run a mix of retrieval-augmented generation stuff and some internal assistants.
[00:13] Priya: Priya, ML lead, mainly responsible for model infra and perf.
[00:16] Jordan: Jordan, infra, networking and private deployments.
[00:19] Marcus: Marcus Chen, SE from Redwood - I own perf benchmarking and runtime tuning.
[00:23] Lina: Cool, agenda is kernel selection, TRT-LLM vs vLLM perf, CUDA graphs, KV cache, batching, quant, and VPC constraints.

[00:35] Marcus: quick orientation - when we talk about vLLM here we mean the vLLM runtime on GPUs (we've seen it used both as a CPU-focused lib and a GPU-targeting one in community forks) versus TensorRT-LLM which compiles attention kernels and fused ops into TRT engines.
[00:47] Priya: we mostly run a 34B dense model, typical prompt lengths 32-128 tokens, and average generation 128 tokens. Our p50 latency requirement is ~150ms for short prompts, p99 is softer but target is <1.2s.
[01:10] Marcus: good, that helps - for those profiles the kernel-launch and small-matrix matmul overheads matter a lot. CUDA Graphs can help a lot for repeated sequences because they reduce per-invocation driver overhead.

[01:30] Jordan: question - how stateful is the KV cache between requests? we do a lot of conversation state and sometimes store multiple sessions in memory.
[01:38] Marcus: Redwood's runtime uses per-session KV cache; the big tradeoffs are memory vs copying overhead. With large context and many concurrent sessions, we either pin the cache on GPU (high memory) or keep it on host and transfer chunks - that's where batching and smart prefix caching helps.

[02:05] Alex: can you give numbers - like tokens/sec and p50 for TRT vs vLLM on g5?
[02:12] Marcus: rough numbers from our lab (34B, fp16, batch=1 with streaming): vLLM (GPU-optimized) p50 ~120ms, p99 ~420ms for 32-token prefixes, tokens/sec ~80-120 depending on prompt. TensorRT-LLM with compiled kernels and CUDA graphs can get p50 down to ~60-90ms and tokens/sec up to 180-240, but that assumes the model compiles cleanly and you accept a longer warmup and potential precision/quantization differences.
[02:46] Priya: warmup is a concern - our traffic is bursty, lots of cold starts. do CUDA graphs exacerbate cold start times?
[02:55] Marcus: yes, there's a compile/warmup phase. CUDA Graphs don't by themselves increase cold-start much, but TRT engine building and autotuning can take minutes. For production we use cached engines and incremental warmup strategies: prewarm a small pool and keep at least one instance warm per model variant.

[03:20] Lina: also noted that TensorRT-LLM often needs extra engineering for custom ops (rotary embeddings, ALiBi, SwiGLU fusions) - Marcus, examples?
[03:29] Marcus: right, some attention variants require custom kernels or fallback to cuBLAS which hurts perf. TRT-LLM's advantage is fused multi-head attention and fused feed-forward. vLLM is more flexible but sometimes runs less-optimal kernels (cuBLAS GEMM) which costs latency. We saw kernel selection differences where TRT's fused attention reduced global memory traffic.

[03:58] [04:00] Alex: what about quantization - we want to push to 4-bit for throughput. tradeoffs?
[04:06] Marcus: TRT supports int8/4-bit via quant-aware calibration pipelines; for 4-bit you'll see big throughput wins (2-3x) but quality regressions depend on the model and calibration dataset. There are also hybrid strategies - keep keys/values in fp16 to preserve attention quality while quantizing weights. vLLM community quant libs (like bitsandbytes) provide 4-bit but on GPU you need kernels that play nicely with the KV cache layout. There are also compatibility headaches with CUDA Graphs and quantized kernels.

[04:45] Priya: KV cache eviction - when you pin a lot of sessions on GPU, do you see fragmentation?
[04:51] Marcus: yes; fragmentation and memory bloat. Redwood's runtime tries to pack KV caches contiguously and uses a pooling allocator. For Nimbus's usage pattern with many concurrent short sessions, a host-resident KV cache with on-demand GPU pinning for hot sessions often wins cost-wise.

[05:20] Jordan: any tips on batching policy? we have latency SLOs and can't blindly increase batch sizes.
[05:26] Marcus: adaptive batching - let short latency-sensitive routes bypass batching or use small max-batch and tight timeouts (1-5ms); background routes (embeddings, offline gen) can have big batches. Also dynamic batch stitching: combine compatible requests by sequence length and pad minimally. Redwood has heuristics to keep p50 tight while improving GPU utilization for p95 traffic.

[05:55] Alex: curious about multi-instance per GPU (MIG-like) or packing multiple models - does Redwood support that?
[06:02] Marcus: we support colocating smaller models and multi-instance scheduling; for big models like 34B we prefer a single instance per GPU for KV cache locality. For quantized models you can sometimes pack N smaller instances depending on memory.
[06:20] Priya: any observed regression at p99 when you enable CUDA graphs?
[06:25] Marcus: sometimes yes - if you over-batch or if the graph was recorded for a specific sequence length distribution it can mis-handle out-of-distribution lengths, so we record multiple graphs per length bucket and fallback to dynamic exec for uncommon sizes. That complexity can show up at p99 if not configured.

[06:50] [07:00] Jordan: networking - for Private deployment we need deterministic latency inside VPC; does Redwood's private runtime require extra egress for model pulls?
[07:07] Lina: Redwood Private can use customer-managed networking and does not force egress for runtime ops. model artifacts can be pulled through customer-controlled storage, and we support KMS/HSM integration for keys.

[07:30] Marcus: i want to call out a measurement we did last quarter: for a 13B model, moving from host-KV to GPU-KV with CUDA graphs reduced p50 by ~30% and doubled tokens/sec at 90% GPU utilization. For 34B that delta shrinks because memory bandwidth dominates.

[08:00] Priya: how do you measure kernel selection? e.g., you said some layers fall back to cuBLAS - do you have per-kernel flamegraphs?
[08:08] Marcus: yes, we collect NVTX ranges and use Nsight Compute/CUPTI to correlate kernels to layers. Redwood's profiler aggregates per-layer time and shows 'hot kernels' and fallback paths. We also capture Python-level stack so you can see where fusions failed.

[08:40] Alex: if we were to run a benchmark, what do you need from us?
[08:45] Marcus: sample model checkpoint (or model spec), representative prompt set (distribution of prefix lengths, generation lengths), target SLOs, and a rough concurrency mix. Also whether you want quant versus fp16 runs.

[09:05] Priya: can you run both vLLM and TRT-LLM side-by-side? we want apples-to-apples comparing final quality and perf.
[09:12] Marcus: yes, we'll run the same workload on both, same batch policy; for TRT we'll record multiple CUDA graphs across sequence buckets. We'll also capture logs for kernel times, memory usage, and KV cache hit/miss rates.

[09:35] [10:00] (discussion digresses briefly into model fusing and rotary embedding variants)

[10:45] Marcus: an important gotcha - TRT-LLM's compilation can change numerics slightly; we recommend a small eval set to ensure outputs are in tol. For some of our enterprise customers we've done a quality-check harness comparing logits/perplexity and downstream evaluation on a sample of production prompts.

[11:15] Alex: about storage for engines - is there a recommended place to store TRT engines within a VPC?
[11:21] Marcus: store them in your private object storage (S3/GCS) with access controlled by role. Redwood Private supports pulling from that storage into local cache nodes, and you can version engines per model/quantization/profile.

[11:40] Priya: what about fallback policies - if TRT engine fails, do you fallback to vLLM or another variant?
[11:46] Marcus: yes, Redwood runtime supports automatic fallback to compatible variants (vLLM fp16 implementation or smaller model) with per-route policies. We also do canary deployments of new engines and soak traffic.

[12:05] Jordan: question on memory pinning and page-locking - does that cause OOMs elsewhere?
[12:11] Marcus: pinned memory reduces transfer latency but reduces available host memory which can cause OOMs for other processes. We recommend bounding pinned pool size and use on-demand pinning for hot KV segments.

[12:40] Priya: are there known issues with cuDNN or cuBLAS versions affecting these fused kernels?
[12:47] Marcus: yes, certain TensorRT and cuDNN combinations lead to different kernel selection and perf. part of our benchmarking includes matrix of CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT versions. we advise standardizing environment in Private deployments.

[13:15] Alex: can you share what a benchmark report looks like?
[13:20] Marcus: we'll produce a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory footprints, per-kernel breakdown, kernel flamegraphs, and a notes section with tuning knobs.

[13:38] (discussion: Priya asks about KV sharding across multiple GPUs)

[13:45] Marcus: KV sharding helps when context is massive - partition KV across devices and route attention accordingly; downside is cross-GPU comm overhead. For multi-GPU within same host NVLink helps. For Nimbus, if you have NVLink-enabled instances, sharding becomes cheaper.

[14:10] [14:30] Alex: we also want to understand operational cost - how do you present cost differences between TRT and vLLM?
[14:16] Marcus: we break down per-token cost using token/sec and instance hour cost. TRT often reduces per-token cost for stable workloads despite higher engineering/warmup cost. vLLM can be cheaper for fragmented, variable traffic because of faster spin-up and less warmup.

[14:40] Priya: any regulatory caveats when using quantized engines or 3rd-party kernels?
[14:45] Marcus: from a data residency perspective nothing changes; from a security/attestation perspective you need to ensure kernels and binaries are vetted. Redwood Private supports supplying your own runtime builds for air-gapped environments.

[15:05] Lina: ok let's walk through the concrete benchmark plan - Marcus?
[15:10] Marcus: propose: 1) Nimbus provides model and sample prompts, 2) Redwood runs fp16 baseline in vLLM, 3) Redwood runs TRT-LLM compile+graph runs, 4) optional quant runs (4-bit) with calibration set, 5) we deliver report and kernel traces. We'll also do a warmup strategy and produce canary configs for production.

[15:40] Alex: timeline?
[15:43] Marcus: we can start once we have artifacts; initial report in 5 business days, quant/extended runs in 10-12 business days.

[15:55] Priya: for the quant runs, do you expect the compaction to change KV layout?
[16:00] Marcus: yes - quantized weight formats sometimes pack values which changes how we store and access KV; we need to ensure KV alignment on 128-bit boundaries for best throughput. That will be part of the low-level profiling.

[16:20] [16:30] (short pause - logistics)

[16:45] Jordan: on the Private deployment side, how do you handle image updates and binary dependencies?
[16:50] Lina: Redwood Private supports customer-managed registries and scheduled updates; we can also do locked-down images and operator-driven rollouts.

[17:05] Marcus: one more perf tip - use multiple recorded CUDA graphs keyed on sequence-length buckets (e.g., 1-16, 17-64, 65-128). We saw a customer improve p99 by 20% by recording three graphs instead of one.

[17:35] Priya: any gotchas with streaming responses and CUDA graphs?
[17:40] Marcus: streaming with CUDA graphs is tricky because streaming implies incremental kernel launches per token; you usually design graphs for the decoding loop and retain the graph state per session. If you want low-latency token streaming you sometimes need a hybrid approach: small decode graphs and on-the-fly kernels for tail tokens.

[18:10] Alex: let's call out specific measurements we'd like: p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU util, memory (GPU+host), per-kernel times, KV hit rate, engine compile time, and quality delta (perplexity/detoks).

[18:30] Marcus: noted. we'll include Nsight/NVTX capture and the raw event logs.

[18:45] Lina: ok wrap up - recap and next steps?
[18:50] Alex: we'll upload the model + prompts by Friday.
[18:53] Priya: yep, aim for Friday.
[18:54] Jordan: i'll capture network constraints and KMS reqs.
[18:56] Marcus: i'll share benchmark scripts and a sample report by Monday.
[19:00] Lina: i'll send Redwood Private security docs and schedule the bench run.
